# **Baseline Energy Standards and Demographic Microdata: An Authoritative Citation and Metadata Registry**

The integration of bottom-up building energy modeling (BEM) with empirical demography represents a critical methodological transition in urban systems planning and grid capacity forecasting.1 Standard engineering practice has long relied on static, deterministic schedules of internal heat gains, occupancy, and appliance usage to assess code compliance and design building systems.3 While these static defaults provide a consistent baseline for regulatory benchmarking, they fail to capture the stochastic, highly variable behaviors that drive peak electricity demand and localized grid congestion.2 To bridge this gap, modern multi-physics and municipal-scale simulations increasingly utilize empirical time-use surveys, census microdata, and demographic projections to construct dynamic, agent-based load profiles.1  
When presenting these hybrid models in peer-reviewed journals, researchers must cite both regulatory baselines and empirical data sources with exact precision. Minor differences in database versions, public-use microdata file (PUMF) iterations, or projection scenario definitions can significantly alter simulation outputs and compromise scientific reproducibility.6 This registry serves as a verified, authoritative reference catalog of the primary standard baselines and national statistics datasets maintained by U.S. and Canadian regulatory bodies.

## **Default Schedules and Deterministic Building Energy Baselines**

In contemporary energy modeling, baseline schedules govern when lights are turned on, when thermostat setpoints shift, and when plug loads draw power.3 Standardizing these parameters is essential for evaluating the energy-saving impacts of updates to building energy codes, such as the International Energy Conservation Code (IECC) or ASHRAE Standard 90.1.4 The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) maintains two primary baseline platforms to support this work: the Prototype Building Models developed by the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) 4 and the programmatic OpenStudio-Standards library managed by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL).10  
The Prototype Building Models represent typical characteristics of approximately 80% of the U.S. commercial and residential building stock.12 PNNL simulates these prototypes across 19 climate locations using EnergyPlus to evaluate the cost-effectiveness and societal impacts of proposed code updates.4 To support these simulations, baseline properties—including envelope thermal resistance, HVAC configurations, and hourly operating schedules—are compiled in official spreadsheet "scorecards".4  
To automate this workflow, the OpenStudio-Standards library programmatically implements these standards.14 Built as a Ruby extension of the OpenStudio Software Development Kit (SDK), this library allows developers to programmatically generate code-compliant baseline models from user-defined geometry templates.11

| Baseline Property | U.S. DOE Commercial & Residential Prototypes | NREL OpenStudio-Standards Library |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Primary Purpose** | Code-effectiveness and policy determination studies 4 | Programmatic baseline generation and compliance checking 16 |
| **Software Platform** | Raw EnergyPlus Input Data Files (.idf) 4 | Programmatic Ruby Gem extending the OpenStudio SDK 11 |
| **Schedule Source** | Standardized hourly Excel scorecards 4 | Programmatic lookup tables in /data/standards/ 14 |
| **Building Types** | 16 commercial/multifamily types; 32 residential configurations 4 | Generates typical templates mapped dynamically to standards 15 |

## **Canadian National Model Codes and Archetype Baselines**

In Canada, building energy codes are designed to establish baseline thermal performance thresholds for building envelopes, HVAC configurations, service hot water systems, and lighting systems.20 These model codes are developed through a consensus-based process managed by the Canadian Commission on Building and Fire Codes (CCBFC) in collaboration with the National Research Council of Canada (NRC) and Natural Resources Canada (NRCan).20 Once enacted, these guidelines serve as the legal foundation for provincial building regulations.24  
For commercial, institutional, and large residential buildings, the National Energy Code of Canada for Buildings (NECB) 2017 establishes critical envelope constraints and system efficiency limits.20 This edition represents a major step toward Canada's goal of achieving Net-Zero Energy Ready (NZER) construction targets by 2030\.24  
For housing and small buildings, Section 9.36 of Division B of the National Building Code of Canada (NBC) 2020 regulates energy compliance.22 This section introduces a tiered energy compliance pathway containing 5 progressive performance tiers, providing a structured regulatory framework to transition standard home construction toward high-efficiency, net-zero ready standards.28

| Compliance Pathway | Target Scope | Compliance Framework | Core Performance Requirements |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **NECB 2017 Prescriptive** 20 | Commercial, institutional, and large multi-unit residential structures 20 | Strict limit compliance per system | Explicit maximum thermal transmittance (![][image1]\-values) for walls, roofs, and fenestration; maximum lighting power density; minimum equipment efficiencies.21 |
| **NBC 2020 Sec 9.36 Tiered Prescriptive** 22 | Housing and small multi-unit buildings (under Part 9\) 22 | Energy conservation points accumulation system | Minimum of 10 performance points achieved through envelope thermal upgrades, window improvements, and high-efficiency mechanical installations.27 |
| **NBC 2020 Sec 9.36 Tiered Performance** 22 | Housing and small multi-unit buildings (under Part 9\) 22 | Whole-building energy modeling comparison | Proposed building must show annual energy consumption and heat loss below the target reference model across five performance tiers.27 |

## **Statistics Canada Empirical Time Use Baselines**

Deterministic code schedules cannot represent the variable behavioral patterns that drive actual residential electricity profiles.2 To capture this variability, stochastic load models use empirical data from the General Social Survey (GSS) Time Use cycles.31 Conducted every five years, these surveys collect 24-hour diaries documenting daily activities, travel patterns, and household demographics for Canadians aged 15 and older.31  
These surveys have evolved significantly over the last two decades.34 While earlier cycles relied on landline telephone frames selected through Random Digit Dialing (RDD), recent iterations use integrated sampling frames that combine landline, cellular, and administrative records.34  
By analyzing these cycles, modelers can characterize changes in domestic routines, work-from-home patterns, and appliance usage.31 This empirical foundation allows researchers to transition BEM load profiles from static code baselines to realistic representations of actual residential demand.2

| GSS Time Use Reference | Core Reference Period | Primary Collection Methods | Sampling Frame Characteristics | Key Behavioral Insights |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Cycle 19: Time Use (2005)** 34 | January – December 2005 34 | Computer-Assisted Telephone Interviewing (CATI) 39 | RDD landline telephone frame, stratified across 27 provincial zones 34 | Baseline pre-smartphone routines, traditional division of unpaid domestic labor, and historical commuting patterns.38 |
| **Cycle 24: Time Stress & Well-Being (2010)** 40 | January – December 2010 40 | CATI telephone interviews 41 | RDD landline telephone frame; excludes cell-only households 41 | Initial collection of secondary/simultaneous child care activities alongside primary diaries.40 |
| **Cycle 29: Time Use (2015)** 7 | April 2015 – April 2016 7 | Multi-mode: CATI and self-administered Electronic Questionnaire (EQ) 7 | Integrated telephone frame combining landline, cell, and census databases 35 | Rapid rise of internet and social media usage; introduction of a streamlined, light time-use diary structure.36 |
| **Time Use Survey (2022)** 37 | July 2022 – July 2023 33 | Multi-mode: CATI telephone and self-administered EQ 7 | Under rebranded GSSP; integrates census, landline, cell, and admin data 35 | Shift toward hybrid work arrangements, post-pandemic home occupant densities, and updated time pressure metrics.33 |

## **Statistics Canada Census and Housing Stock Characterization**

To scale individual home simulations up to represent entire neighborhoods or cities, models must reflect localized housing stock characteristics.2 The Public Use Microdata Files (PUMFs) from the Statistics Canada Census of Population provide the necessary demographic and structural detail.45 These files allow researchers to correlate resident characteristics with structural variables to identify and model common regional housing archetypes.2  
The 2021 Census offers two primary PUMF releases: the Individuals File and the Hierarchical File.6 The Individuals File contains a ![][image2] sample of anonymous census records across 144 social and demographic variables.48 To protect privacy, geographic identifiers are restricted to provinces/territories and census metropolitan areas.48  
The Hierarchical File provides a ![][image3] sample of Canadian households.49 This file allows researchers to analyze nested relationships, such as evaluating structural dwelling characteristics and localized shelter costs directly alongside individual household member demographics.6

| Census PUMF Product | Microdata Sample Size | Core Housing & Dwelling Variables | Primary Structural Features | Geographic Identifiers |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **2021 Census Individuals File** 48 | ![][image2] sample of anonymized Canadian census responses 48 | Dwelling type, household size, construction period, primary heating fuel, tenure 47 | Cross-sectional micro-level correlation of demographic variables with dwelling types 47 | Provinces, territories, and major Census Metropolitan Areas (CMAs) 48 |
| **2021 Census Hierarchical File** 49 | ![][image4] sample of anonymous Canadian households 49 | Nested dwelling units, monthly shelter costs, rent status, household income metrics 6 | Direct nesting of individual occupant records within household-level housing envelopes 46 | Restricted provincial and large metropolitan boundaries 6 |

## **Demographic Projections and Grid Load Modeling**

Changes in population size and structure directly alter residential energy consumption profiles.52 To plan for future energy infrastructure, researchers inject long-term demographic shifts into bottom-up building models.1 These projections are developed by Statistics Canada's Centre for Demography using a cohort-component projection model.53  
Socio-demographic patterns in Canada are highly sensitive to policy changes and migration trends.54 The latest projections, released on January 27, 2026, use 2025 population estimates as their baseline.53 These projections incorporate recent shifts in immigration targets, temporary resident policies, and post-pandemic fertility trends.54  
The projections cover ten scenarios: low-growth, high-growth, slow-aging, fast-aging, and six medium-growth (M1 through M6) scenarios that reflect different interprovincial migration patterns.53 The M1 scenario serves as the primary national baseline.53 It incorporates a medium total fertility rate, medium mortality assumptions, and a medium interprovincial migration rate derived from a 25-year historical average.53

| Projection Scenario | Base Population Year | Fertility Assumption | Mortality Assumption | Immigration Targets | Non-Permanent Residents | Interprovincial Migration Assumption |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **M1 (Medium-Growth Scenario)** 53 | 2025 53 | Medium: Total fertility rate stabilizes at 1.32 by 2049 53 | Medium: Aligned with long-term average life expectancy projections 53 | Medium: Reflects updated permanent resident targets 53 | Medium: Aligned with temporary resident caps and targets 53 | 10-year transition from 2022–25 rates to the 2000–25 average; constant after 2034\.53 |
| **LG (Low-Growth Scenario)** 53 | 2025 53 | Low: Total fertility rate stabilizes at 1.09 by 2049 53 | High: Higher projected mortality rates 53 | Low: Assumes lower permanent immigration 53 | Low: Assumes lower temporary resident counts 53 | Aligned with the M1 interprovincial migration rate model.53 |
| **HG (High-Growth Scenario)** 53 | 2025 53 | High: Total fertility rate stabilizes at 1.55 by 2049 53 | Low: Lower projected mortality rates 53 | High: Assumes higher permanent immigration 53 | High: Assumes higher temporary resident counts 53 | Aligned with the M1 interprovincial migration rate model.53 |

## **Empirical Residential Energy Calibration Benchmarks**

To ensure bottom-up residential simulation results align with actual energy consumption, modelers calibrate their load profiles against regional benchmarks.2 In Canada, this reference baseline is provided by the Survey of Household Energy Use (SHEU), which is conducted jointly by Natural Resources Canada and Statistics Canada.32 The survey collects detailed energy data from approximately 15 million households to establish energy intensity baselines across different regions and dwelling types.32  
The SHEU 2019 reveals that space and water heating account for 81% of total residential energy consumption in Canada.52 This thermal load is met primarily by natural gas (![][image5]) and electricity (![][image6]).32  
For end-use calibration, modelers must reference specific thematic tables within the SHEU data structure.58 This allows researchers to isolate and calibrate specific load categories, such as baseline appliance draws, electronics loads, and lighting system usage.58

| Residential Calibration Field | SHEU 2019 Key Technical Insights | Primary Fuel Shares | Regional Intensity Range | Key Calibration Data Tables |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Space & Water Heating** 52 | Accounts for ![][image7] of Canadian household energy use.52 Furnaces (![][image8]) and baseboards (![][image9]) are the dominant systems.32 | Natural Gas: ![][image5] Electricity: ![][image6] Oil/Wood: ![][image10].32 | National average: 98.1 GJ per household. Ranges from 85.2 in Atlantic Canada to 124.8 in Alberta.32 | Section 6 (Tables 6.1a to 6.5b) 58 and Section 9 (Tables 9.1a & 9.1b).58 |
| **Appliances & Electronics** 52 | Refrigerator saturation is high; ![][image11] of households own a secondary unit.32 Televisions (![][image12]) and computers (![][image13]) drive plug loads.32 | Electricity: ![][image14] of active mechanical appliance draw.32 | Electricity average: 39.8 GJ per household. Ranges from 24.2 in Alberta to 63.9 in Quebec.32 | Section 10 (Tables 10.1a to 10.9b) 58 and Section 11 (Tables 11.1a to 11.10b).58 |
| **Lighting Systems** 52 | LED light bulbs are used in ![][image15] of households, followed by traditional incandescent bulbs (![][image16]).32 | Electricity: ![][image14] of active lamp draw.32 | Overall lighting consumption metrics are nested within electricity intensity totals.58 | Section 12 (Tables 12.1a to 12.2b).58 |
